title: Single Slit Diffraction
lead: Light passing through one slit interferes with itself, because every part of the slit sends out wavelets of its own. The pattern it makes on a screen has a broad, bright central maximum with much dimmer and narrower maxima on either side. This section explains where the dark minima fall, at angles where the width of the slit times the sine of the angle is a whole number of wavelengths, and uses that condition to find the width of a slit.
objectives: Discuss the single slit diffraction pattern.
summary_html:
• A single slit produces an interference pattern characterized by a broad central maximum with narrower and dimmer maxima to the sides.
  • There is destructive interference for a single slit when $\kDslit\;\text{sin}\;\theta = m\klam\;\text{(for}\;m=1,\;-1,\;2,\;-2,\;3,\;\ldots)$, where $\kDslit$ is the slit width, $\klam$ is the light’s wavelength, $\theta$ is the angle relative to the original direction of the light, and $m$ is the order of the minimum. Note that there is no $m=0$ minimum.
notes: Two conceptual questions are set here from other sections: the pattern of red dots that shows single slit as well as double slit interference, with its photograph, from Section 27.3, and the single slit with no minimum, from Section 27.4. Seven of the module’s fourteen problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the first minima of 410-nm and 700-nm light through a slit 2.00 μm wide, the slit width and wavelength for first minima at 60.0° and 62.0°, the wavelength with a first minimum at 36.9°, the third minimum of 633-nm light through a slit 20.0 μm wide, the smallest slit widths for one, 50 and 1000 minima, the ratio of slit width to separation that removes the fifth double slit maximum, and the first minimum of sound through a hangar door.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 27.21) (a) Single slit diffraction pattern. Monochromatic light passing through a single slit has a central maximum and many smaller and dimmer maxima on either side. The central maximum is six times higher than shown. (b) The drawing shows the bright central maximum and dimmer and thinner maxima on either side. (Figure 27.23) A graph of single slit diffraction intensity showing the central maximum to be wider and much more intense than those to the sides. In fact the central maximum is six times higher than shown here.

(Figure 27.22) Light passing through a single slit is diffracted in all directions and may interfere constructively or destructively, depending on the angle. The difference in path length for rays from either side of the slit is seen to be $D\sin\theta$. (Figure 27.24) A graph of the single slit diffraction pattern is analyzed in this example.

exercises.prompt: A diffraction pattern is formed on a screen when light of wavelength 410 nm is passed through a single slit of width 1 μm. If the source light is replaced by another light of wavelength 700 nm, what should be the width of the slit so that the new light produces a pattern with the same spacing?

answer.hint: The minima stay at the same angles when $\klam/\kDslit$ stays the same, so the slit width must grow in proportion to the wavelength.

exercises.prompt: Monochromatic light passing through a single slit forms a diffraction pattern on a screen. If the second minimum occurs at an angle of 15°, find the angle for the fourth minimum.

answer.solution: The minima satisfy $\kDslit\sin\theta = m\klam$, so $\sin\theta$ is proportional to the order $m$. The fourth minimum therefore has twice the sine of the second: $\sin\theta_4 = 2\sin 15^\circ = 2(0.259) = 0.518$, and $\theta_4 = \sin^{-1} 0.518 = 31.2^\circ$. Note that the angle is a little more than twice 15°, because it is the sine, not the angle, that doubles.

exercises.prompt: As the width of the slit producing a single-slit diffraction pattern is reduced, how will the diffraction pattern produced change?

answer.solution: The pattern spreads out. The minima lie where $\sin\theta = m\klam/\kDslit$, so a smaller slit width $\kDslit$ gives a larger $\sin\theta$ for every minimum, and the central maximum and the dimmer maxima beside it all grow wider. When the slit becomes as narrow as the wavelength, the first minimum reaches 90° and the central maximum fills the whole screen. Less light also gets through the narrower slit, so the pattern is dimmer.

figure.alt: A horizontal line of equally spaced red dots of light on a black background. The central dot is the brightest, the dots fade almost to nothing six dots to either side, brighten a little beyond, and fade again twelve and eighteen dots from the center.
figure.caption: This double slit interference pattern also shows signs of single slit interference. (credit: PASCO)

exercises.prompt: The figure shows the central part of the interference pattern for a pure wavelength of red light projected onto a double slit. The pattern is actually a combination of single slit and double slit interference. Note that the bright spots are evenly spaced. Is this a double slit or single slit characteristic? Note that some of the bright spots are dim on either side of the center. Is this a single slit or double slit characteristic? Which is smaller, the slit width or the separation between slits? Explain your responses.

answer.solution: The even spacing of the bright spots is a double slit characteristic: the double slit maxima lie at $\kd\sin\theta = m\klam$, evenly spaced for small angles. The dimming of some spots on either side of the center is a single slit characteristic: each slit alone makes a pattern with minima at $\kDslit\sin\theta = m\klam$, and where one of those minima falls, the double slit spots are nearly wiped out. The single slit minima fall at about every sixth spot, so they are about six times farther apart than the double slit maxima. Since the spacing of a pattern grows as the slit dimension shrinks, the slit width is the smaller of the two, about one sixth of the separation between the slits.

exercises.prompt: It is possible that there is no minimum in the interference pattern of a single slit. Explain why. Is the same true of double slits and diffraction gratings?

answer.solution: The first minimum of a single slit lies where $\sin\theta = \klam/\kDslit$. If the slit is narrower than the wavelength, $\klam/\kDslit$ is greater than 1, no angle has that sine, and there is no minimum at all: the light spreads from the slit with its intensity falling off smoothly. The same is true of double slits and gratings. Their first minimum lies at $\kd\sin\theta = \klam/2$, so if the slits are closer together than half a wavelength there is no minimum either, and only the central maximum remains.

exercises.prompt: (a) At what angle is the first minimum for 550-nm light falling on a single slit of width 1.00 μm? (b) Will there be a second minimum?

answer.part: (a) the angle of the first minimum
answer.hint: Set $m = 1$ in $\kDslit\sin\theta = m\klam$; for part (b), ask whether $\sin\theta = 2\klam/\kDslit$ can be less than 1.

exercises.prompt: (a) How wide is a single slit that produces its first minimum for 633-nm light at an angle of 28.0°? (b) At what angle will the second minimum be?

parts.part: (b) the angle of the second minimum
parts.hint: With the width known, set $m = 2$ and solve for $\theta$.

exercises.prompt: Find the wavelength of light that has its third minimum at an angle of 48.6° when it falls on a single slit of width 3.00 μm.
(a) Sodium vapor light averaging 589 nm in wavelength falls on a single slit of width 7.50 μm. At what angle does it produces its second minimum? (b) What is the highest-order minimum produced?

parts.part: (a) the angle of the second minimum

parts.hint: The highest order is the largest whole number $m$ for which $m\klam/\kDslit$ is still less than 1.

exercises.prompt: (a) Find the angle between the first minima for the two sodium vapor lines, which have wavelengths of 589.1 and 589.6 nm, when they fall upon a single slit of width 2.00 μm. (b) What is the distance between these minima if the diffraction pattern falls on a screen 1.00 m from the slit? (c) Discuss the ease or difficulty of measuring such a distance.

parts.part: (a) the angle between the first minima
parts.hint: Find the angle of the first minimum for each wavelength and subtract, keeping enough digits that the small difference survives.
Each minimum lies at a distance $\tan\theta$ times 1.00 m from the center of the screen; subtract the two.

answer.solution:
(a) $0.0150^\circ$

(b) 0.262 mm

(c) This distance is not easily measured by human eye, but under a microscope or magnifying glass it is quite easily measurable.

exercises.prompt: (a) If a single slit produces a first minimum at 14.5°, at what angle is the second-order minimum? (b) What is the angle of the third-order minimum? (c) Is there a fourth-order minimum? (d) Use your answers to illustrate how the angular width of the central maximum is about twice the angular width of the next maximum (which is the angle between the first and second minima).

Integrated Concepts A water break at the entrance to a harbor consists of a rock barrier with a 50.0-m-wide opening. Ocean waves of 20.0-m wavelength approach the opening straight on. At what angle to the incident direction are the boats inside the harbor most protected against wave action?

parts.hint: The opening acts as a single slit, so the calm directions are the minima, $\kDslit\sin\theta = m\klam$ with $m = 1$.
Repeat with $m = 2$; a third minimum would need $\sin\theta$ greater than 1.
